A Mathematical Theory of Top-k Sparse Attention via Total Variation Distance

Georgios Tzachristas    Lei Deng    Ioannis Tzachristas    Gong Zhang    Renhai Chen
1 Theory Laboratory, Central Research Institute, 2012 Laboratory,
Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, China.
{tzachristasgeorgios, deng.lei2, nicholas.zhang, chenrenhai}@huawei.com
2 National Technical University of Athens, Greece
el23102@mail.ntua.gr
3 Trustworthy Technology and Engineering Laboratory, Heisenberg Research Center,
2012 Laboratory, Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., Munich, Germany.
ioannis.tzachristas@huawei.com
Abstract

We develop a unified mathematical framework for certified Top-kk attention truncation that quantifies approximation error at both the distribution and output levels. For a single attention distribution PP and its Top-kk truncation P^\hat{P}, we show that the total-variation distance coincides with the discarded softmax tail mass and satisfies the exact identity

TV(P,P^)=1−e−KL(P^∥P),\operatorname{TV}(P,\hat{P})=1-e^{-\operatorname{KL}(\hat{P}\|P)},

replacing generic inequalities by a sharp equality specific to Top-kk truncation. Building on this, we derive a hierarchy of non-asymptotic deterministic bounds—from a single boundary gap, through multi-gap and blockwise variants—that control TV⁡(P,P^)\operatorname{TV}(P,\hat{P}) using only the ordered logits.

We then turn to the attention outputs. Using an exact head–tail decomposition, we prove that the vector error factorizes as

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk​(q,K,V)‖2=τ​‖μtail−μhead‖2,τ=TV⁡(P,P^),\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\mathrm{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\|_{2}=\tau\,\|\mu_{\text{tail}}-\mu_{\text{head}}\|_{2},\hskip 20.00003pt\tau=\operatorname{TV}(P,\hat{P}),

yielding a new head–tail diameter bound

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk​(q,K,V)‖2≤τ​diamH,T,\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\mathrm{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\|_{2}\leq\tau\,\mathrm{diam}_{H,T},

where diamH,T\mathrm{diam}_{H,T} is the cross-set diameter of the value vectors. This introduces the value matrix VV as an explicit geometric parameter in the error bound, and we further obtain variance-based refinements that relate the output error to VarP⁡(V)\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V).

Under an i.i.d. Gaussian score model si∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)s_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), we derive closed-form expressions for the softmax tail mass and show that the minimal kεk_{\varepsilon} ensuring TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\hat{P})\leq\varepsilon obeys an asymptotic design rule kε/n≈Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(ε))k_{\varepsilon}/n\approx\Phi_{c}(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)). These analytical results motivate two certified selection algorithms, Δk\Delta_{k}-Search and MC-Search, which adaptively score only a subset of keys and stop as soon as they can certify that a prescribed Top-kk truncation satisfies TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon.

Empirical evaluations on bert-base-uncased attention maps and synthetic long-context logits confirm the predicted scaling of the certified sparsity ratio kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n, reveal heavier-tailed logits than the Gaussian idealization, and demonstrate that certified Top-kk can reduce scored keys by a factor of 22–4×4\times on average—and by orders of magnitude on sharply peaked heads—while rigorously respecting the prescribed total-variation error.

Keywords: Top-k attention, certified sparsification, total-variation bounds, softmax truncation, probabilistic analysis, efficient transformers

1 Introduction

The attention mechanism is the computational core of modern transformer architectures. For a sequence of nn tokens with query, key, and value representations Q,K∈ℝn×dQ,K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and V∈ℝn×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{v}}, the standard attention operator

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤d)​V\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\softmax\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V

requires O⁡(n2​d)O(n^{2}d) time and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory to compute, dominated by the pairwise dot products between all queries and keys. As the context length nn grows into the tens or hundreds of thousands, this quadratic scaling has become the primary bottleneck in large language models (LLMs).

A natural remedy is to exploit the observation that, for each query, only a small number of keys contribute significantly to the attention output. Top-kk sparse attention methods approximate the softmax weights by, for each query qiq_{i}, retaining only the kk largest scores qi⊤​kjq_{i}^{\top}k_{j} over jj and zeroing the rest. Such sparsity can lead to subquadratic complexity and aligns well with modern hardware, and numerous practical variants have been proposed, including block-based, hierarchical, and hash-based sparse attention. Several mainstream open-source systems now adopt Top-kk sparse attention in their inference stacks.

Despite impressive empirical performance, however, the mathematical foundations of these methods remain poorly understood. In this work we study Top-kk attention truncation through the lens of probability and optimization. Fundamental questions persist:

  • •

    How does truncating the softmax affect the output distribution and the resulting attention output?

  • •

    What deterministic or probabilistic guarantees can bound the error introduced by keeping only the top kk keys?

  • •

    Can we design algorithms that certify in advance that a given truncation achieves a desired accuracy?

1.1 Contributions

This paper develops a unified mathematical theory of Top-kk attention that quantifies the effect of truncation at both the distribution and output levels, and connects these guarantees to certified sparse-attention algorithms. Our main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Distribution-level theory for Top-kk truncation. For a softmax distribution PP and its Top-kk truncation P^\widehat{P}, we show that the total-variation distance coincides with the discarded softmax tail mass and satisfies the exact identity

    TV(P,P^)= 1−e−KL(P^∥P).\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;=\;1-e^{-\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\,\|\,P)}.

    This replaces generic inequality-based bounds with a sharp equality specific to Top-kk truncation and serves as the foundation for all subsequent certificates.

  2. 2.

    Deterministic certificates from score gaps and blocks. Using only the ordered logits s1≥⋯≥sns_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}, we derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on TV⁡(P,P^)\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P}) in terms of: (i) a single boundary gap sk−sk+1s_{k}-s_{k+1}; (ii) multi-gap (pigeonhole) refinements; and (iii) blockwise extensions that operate on groups of consecutive keys. These results yield a hierarchy of deterministic certificates, from fine-grained to coarse-grained, without any distributional assumptions.

  3. 3.

    Output-level error bounds and geometry of the value matrix. We establish an exact head–tail decomposition

    ‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2=τ​‖μtail−μhead‖2,τ=TV⁡(P,P^),\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\;=\;\tau\,\bigl\|\mu_{\text{tail}}-\mu_{\text{head}}\bigr\|_{2},\hskip 20.00003pt\tau=\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P}),

    and obtain a new head–tail diameter bound

    ‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤τ​diamH,T,\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\;\leq\;\tau\,\mathrm{diam}_{H,T},

    where diamH,T\mathrm{diam}_{H,T} is the cross-set diameter of the value vectors. This introduces the value matrix VV as an explicit geometric parameter in the error and is complemented by variance-based bounds that relate the output error to VarP⁡(V)\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V). We further give a graph-theoretic characterization of the optimal head–tail partition: the "minimax" cross diameter is achieved by cutting the lightest edge of a maximum spanning tree.

  4. 4.

    Probabilistic laws under a Gaussian score model. Under an i.i.d. Gaussian model si∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)s_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), we derive closed-form expressions for the softmax tail mass and show that the minimal kεk_{\varepsilon} ensuring TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon obeys an asymptotic design rule

    kε/n≈Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(ε)).k_{\varepsilon}/n\;\approx\;\Phi_{c}\bigl(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)\bigr).

    This links error tolerance, logit variance, and expected sparsity, providing a principled guideline for choosing kk in high-dimensional regimes.

  5. 5.

    Certified selection algorithms and empirical validation. We translate these analytical results into two certified Top-kk selection procedures: Δk\Delta_{k}-Search, which uses a gap-based certificate, and MC-Search, which uses mass certificates and their blockwise extensions. Both algorithms adaptively score only as many keys as needed to certify TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon, with Δk\Delta_{k}-Search verifying a prescribed Top-kk and MC-Search additionally returning the minimal mass-certified size kε​(q)k_{\varepsilon}(q) for each query.

    Experiments on bert-base-uncased attention maps and synthetic long-context logits confirm the predicted scaling of the certified sparsity ratio kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n, reveal heavier-tailed logits than the Gaussian idealization, and demonstrate that certified Top-kk can reduce the number of scored keys by factors of 22–4×4\times on average, and by orders of magnitude for sharply peaked heads, while rigorously respecting the prescribed TV budget.

1.2 Applications to LLM-based systems

The theory developed here enables provably efficient attention in practical LLM deployments. By coupling the exact tail-mass identity

TV(P,P^)=1−e−KL(P^∥P)\mathrm{TV}(P,\hat{P})=1-e^{-\mathrm{KL}(\hat{P}\,\|\,P)}

with our certified selectors (Δk\Delta_{k}-Search and MC-Search), one can adaptively choose the minimal Top-kk per head and query that meets a prescribed tolerance ε\varepsilon, potentially yielding subquadratic complexity in the sequence length with explicit accuracy guarantees (Sections 4–7). The same certificates extend to structured, blockwise pruning across heads, windows, or tiles, supporting head/window selection under verifiable error budgets (Sections 4 and 7). Because the certification is orthogonal to implementation, it composes with fast attention kernels to reduce FLOPs without altering semantics, and it can inform serving-time trade-offs (latency/throughput vs. bounded deviation) as well as training-time objectives that encourage larger score gaps or target TV budgets. Empirically, certified sparsity scales predictably with context length while preserving the requested bound, making the approach suitable for long-context inference and resource-constrained deployment (Sections 7–8).

1.3 Scope and Structure

Our analysis focuses on single-head attention with fixed queries, but the results extend naturally to multi-head settings and to other exponential-family attention mechanisms. The paper is organized as follows. Section 3 introduces notation and basic definitions. Section 4 derives fundamental identities connecting total variation, KL divergence, and related quantities, and establishes deterministic gap and blockwise bounds. Section 5 converts these distribution-level guarantees into output-level error guarantees, including geometric and graph-theoretic characterizations of the value matrix. Section 6 develops probabilistic predictions under a Gaussian score model. Section 7 presents certified selection algorithms translating these bounds into practice. Section 8 empirically validates the theory on real attention maps and synthetic long-context logits. Section 9 concludes with a discussion of implications, limitations, and future directions.

In summary, this work provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for Top-kk attention, showing that its empirical robustness follows from the precise exponential decay of the discarded softmax mass and from structural properties of the value vectors, and that these insights enable the design of attention mechanisms with certified accuracy guarantees.

2 Related Work

The quadratic time and memory complexity of the standard attention operator has motivated extensive research into efficient and sparse alternatives. A full attention layer requires O⁡(n2​d)O(n^{2}d) computation, which becomes prohibitive for long sequences. Consequently, a wide variety of methods have sought to approximate or restrict the attention pattern while preserving model quality. Most of these approaches rely on heuristic sparsity or low-rank assumptions, and even when they come with theoretical guarantees, these are usually stated in terms of kernel or matrix approximation or model expressivity rather than per-query accuracy of the attention distribution. Our work differs in offering a unified mathematical analysis of Top-kk truncation with provable, certified error bounds on the resulting softmax distribution.

Fixed and Learned Sparse Patterns.

Early efforts such as the Sparse Transformer [1] introduced fixed blockwise and strided attention masks that reduce complexity while maintaining global context. Subsequent models, including Longformer [2] and BigBird [3], combined local sliding windows with a small number of global tokens to extend attention to thousands of tokens. These methods improve scalability and can be trained effectively, but they impose hard-coded sparsity patterns rather than deriving them from the attention statistics themselves. They do not, however, provide explicit per-query deterministic or probabilistic bounds on the approximation error introduced by truncating a given attention distribution.

Low-Rank and Kernel Approximations.

A second line of work compresses the attention matrix through low-rank or kernel-based approximations. Linformer [4] projects the key and value matrices into a lower-dimensional subspace, achieving linear complexity in sequence length. Performer [5] and Random Feature Attention [8] replace the softmax kernel by positive random feature maps, while Nyströmformer [6] approximates the attention matrix using Nyström sampling. These techniques provide substantial speedups and are accompanied by theoretical analyses in terms of kernel or matrix approximation error, or unbiasedness and concentration of the underlying estimators. However, their guarantees typically concern approximation of the attention kernel or matrix, rather than explicit per-query bounds on the deviation between the approximate and exact softmax distributions that can be turned into certification rules. In contrast, our analysis derives closed-form deterministic and probabilistic guarantees on the deviation between the truncated and exact softmax distributions.

Memory-Efficient Implementations.

Complementary work has focused on optimizing the exact softmax computation for modern hardware. FlashAttention [7] reorganizes the computation to minimize GPU memory access, achieving large throughput gains without altering the mathematical definition of attention. While such systems-level improvements are orthogonal to sparsification, our certified truncation algorithms can be combined with such implementations to yield both theoretical and practical efficiency.

Analytical and Theoretical Perspectives.

Several studies have examined the softmax function from a numerical or probabilistic viewpoint. Classical works on exponential families and on regular variation [9, 10] provide the probabilistic foundation for our Gaussian score model analysis. Despite these advances, prior work stops short of delivering exact identities or certifiable algorithms that bound, for a given finite score set, the total-variation error arising from truncating the attention distribution.

Position of This Work.

Our contribution is orthogonal and complementary to these lines of research. We develop, to our knowledge, the first rigorous closed-form TV/KL-based mathematical theory of Top-kk attention truncation, proving an exact identity between total-variation distance and KL divergence, deriving deterministic and Gaussian-model bounds, and translating them into Δk\Delta_{k}-Search and MC-Search algorithms that certify a desired accuracy (TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon) before computing all dot products. Whereas most existing methods trade accuracy for speed heuristically or provide only kernel-level approximation guarantees, our framework provides verifiable per-query guarantees linking sparsity, score variance, and approximation error—establishing a principled foundation for provably correct sparse attention.

Comparative Guarantees.

Most existing efficient-attention architectures—including Linformer [4], Performer [5], Reformer [11], and other kernelized or low-rank variants—reduce computational cost by projecting or approximating the attention kernel. Their analyses typically provide bounds on kernel or matrix approximation error, or characterize unbiasedness and concentration of random feature estimators, rather than giving explicit per-query bounds (for example, in total-variation distance) on the deviation between the approximate and true softmax distributions that can be used as certification rules for a particular score vector.

In contrast, our framework establishes finite-sample, non-asymptotic guarantees in total-variation distance. The exact identity

TV(P,P^)=1−e−KL(P^∥P)\mathrm{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=1-e^{-\mathrm{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)}

for the pair (P,P^)(P,\widehat{P}) arising from Top-kk truncation links the truncation error directly to discarded softmax mass, yielding deterministic certificates that hold for any finite score set. Unlike prior methods, our certified algorithms (Δk\Delta_{k}-Search and MC-Search) guarantee that the truncated attention achieves TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon before any approximation is accepted. Thus, the proposed theory replaces heuristic sparsity with verifiable correctness, complementing empirically efficient methods with provable accuracy control.

3 Preliminaries and Notation

We formalize the notation and definitions used throughout the paper and record several basic properties of the softmax and its Top-kk truncation.

3.1 Attention Scores and Softmax Probabilities

For a single query vector q∈ℝdq\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, keys k1,…,kn∈ℝdk_{1},\dots,k_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and values v1,…,vn∈ℝdvv_{1},\dots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, define the (scaled) similarity scores

si=q⊤​kid,i=1,…,n.s_{i}=\frac{q^{\top}k_{i}}{\sqrt{d}},\hskip 20.00003pti=1,\dots,n.
Indexing convention.

For each query qq, let π\pi be a permutation that sorts the scores in non-increasing order: s(1)≥⋯≥s(n)s_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq s_{(n)} with s(i)=sπ⁡(i)s_{(i)}=s_{\pi(i)}. From now on we relabel indices by π\pi and drop parentheses, so that s1≥⋯≥sns_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}, and the associated pairs (ki,vi)(k_{i},v_{i}) are reindexed accordingly. Ties are broken by a fixed rule (e.g., smaller original index). All sums over indices 1:k1{:}k (e.g., ∑i=1k\sum_{i=1}^{k}) use this convention.

The standard softmax probabilities are

pi=esi∑j=1nesj,P=(p1,…,pn),p_{i}=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}},\hskip 20.00003ptP=(p_{1},\dots,p_{n}),

which define a discrete distribution on {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}.

We also collect the keys and values into matrices

K:=[k1⊤kn⊤]∈ℝn×dandV:=[v1⊤vn⊤]∈ℝn×dv.K:=\begin{bmatrix}k_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ k_{n}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002ptV:=\begin{bmatrix}v_{1}^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ v_{n}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{v}}.

For a single query corresponding to a row q⊤q^{\top} of QQ, we view qq as a column vector and specialize the matrix formula

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤d)​V\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\softmax\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V

to

Attn⁡(q,K,V)=V⊤​softmax⁡(K​qd)=∑i=1npi​vi.\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)=V^{\top}\softmax\!\left(\frac{Kq}{\sqrt{d}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}v_{i}.

This requires computing all nn dot products q⊤​kiq^{\top}k_{i}.

3.2 Top-kk Truncation

For a fixed integer k<nk<n, let Ik={1,…,k}I_{k}=\{1,\ldots,k\}. The Top-kk truncated distribution is

p^i={esi∑j=1kesj,for ​i≤k,0,for ​i>k,P^=(p^1,…,p^n).\widehat{p}_{i}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{e^{s_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{s_{j}}},&\text{for }i\leq k,\\[8.0pt] 0,&\text{for }i>k,\end{cases}\hskip 20.00003pt\widehat{P}=(\widehat{p}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{p}_{n}).

The corresponding truncated attention output is

Attnk⁡(q,K,V):=∑i=1kp^i​vi.\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V):=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\widehat{p}_{i}\,v_{i}.

3.3 Error Measures and Basic Properties

We quantify the distance between the full distribution PP and its truncated version P^\widehat{P} using standard divergences and record several elementary properties that will be used throughout.

Total variation.
TV⁡(P,P^)=12​∑i=1n|pi−p^i|.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|p_{i}-\widehat{p}_{i}|.
Kullback–Leibler divergence.
KL(P^∥P)=∑i=1np^ilogp^ipi.\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{p}_{i}\log\!\frac{\widehat{p}_{i}}{p_{i}}.

We adopt the standard convention 0​log⁡(0/q)=00\log(0/q)=0 for q>0q>0, since limx↓0x​log⁡(x/q)=0\lim_{x\downarrow 0}x\log(x/q)=0.

Because p^i=0\widehat{p}_{i}=0 for i>ki>k, the divergence KL(P∥P^)\operatorname{KL}(P\|\widehat{P}) is infinite unless the truncation error is zero, whereas KL(P^∥P)\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P) remains finite and is therefore used throughout.

Basic properties.
  • •

    Shift invariance: For any constant c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, replacing every score sis_{i} by si+cs_{i}+c leaves PP and P^\widehat{P} unchanged.

  • •

    Normalization: ∑ipi=∑ip^i=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=\sum_{i}\widehat{p}_{i}=1.

  • •

    Ordering convention: (s1,…,sn)(s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}) always refers to scores sorted in non-increasing order.

3.4 Notation Summary

4 Distribution-Level Theory of Top-kk Truncation

In this section we study the effect of Top-kk truncation purely at the level of the softmax distribution. We first establish two fundamental identities relating the truncation error in total variation and KL divergence, and then derive deterministic upper bounds that depend only on simple score statistics (gaps and block masses).

4.1 Tail–Mass Identity for Total Variation

The most immediate consequence of truncation is that the total variation (TV) distance between PP and P^\widehat{P} equals the probability mass that is removed from the tail.

Lemma 4.1 (Tail–mass identity).

For Top-kk truncation as above,

TV⁡(P,P^)=∑i>kpi.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\sum_{i>k}p_{i}.

Proof. See Appendix A.1.

Remark 4.2 (Shift invariance).

For any constant c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, replacing every score sis_{i} by si+cs_{i}+c leaves both PP and P^\widehat{P} unchanged, since each is normalized by the same exponential factor ece^{c}. Consequently, all subsequent results depend only on score differences, such as gaps si−sjs_{i}-s_{j}, and are invariant to global shifts of the score vector.

4.2 Exact Relationship Between TV and KL Divergence

Building on the tail–mass identity, we next show that the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the truncated and full distributions admits a closed-form expression, leading to an exact exponential relationship with the total-variation distance.

Theorem 4.3 (Exact TV–KL identity).

For the distributions PP and P^\widehat{P} defined above,

KL(P^∥P)=log∑j=1nesj∑j=1kesj,TV(P,P^)=1−e−KL(P^∥P).\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)=\log\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{s_{j}}},\hskip 20.00003pt\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=1-e^{-\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)}.
Proof.

See Appendix A.2. ∎

Remark 4.4 (Asymmetry of the KL direction).

The divergence KL(P∥P^)\operatorname{KL}(P\|\widehat{P}) is infinite unless the discarded tail mass is zero, because p^i=0\widehat{p}_{i}=0 for i>ki>k. The finite quantity KL(P^∥P)\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P) therefore provides the meaningful asymmetric comparison for truncated softmax distributions.

4.3 Consequences

Theorem A.2 reveals that the truncation error measured by total variation is exactly the complement of an exponential in the KL divergence. Thus the two measures are not merely related by an inequality (as in Pinsker’s bound), but by an identity specific to Top-kk truncation of a normalized exponential family.

Moreover, for small tail mass τ=TV⁡(P,P^)≪1\tau=\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\ll 1, the expansion

KL(P^∥P)=−log(1−τ)=τ+O(τ2)\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)=-\log(1-\tau)=\tau+O(\tau^{2})

shows that KL\operatorname{KL} and TV\operatorname{TV} coincide to first order. Consequently, either quantity can serve as a mathematically precise proxy for truncation error, depending on analytical convenience.

4.4 Deterministic Bounds via Score Gaps and Blocks

The exact TV\operatorname{TV}–KL\operatorname{KL} identity of Theorem A.2 expresses the truncation error as a function of exponential sums over all nn scores. While this form is precise, it still depends on the entire score vector. In this subsection we derive deterministic bounds that depend only on simple quantities—notably the boundary gap

Δk=sk−sk+1,\Delta_{k}\;=\;s_{k}-s_{k+1},

and, more generally, aggregated block gaps. These bounds provide computable and interpretable certificates of small truncation error.

4.4.1 A Pointwise Gap Bound

Theorem 4.5 (Deterministic gap bound).

Assume the scores are ordered s1≥⋯≥sns_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}, and define Δk:=sk−sk+1\Delta_{k}:=s_{k}-s_{k+1}. Then the total-variation error of Top-kk truncation satisfies

TV⁡(P,P^)≤(n−k)​esk+1k​esk+(n−k)​esk+1=11+kn−k​eΔk.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\frac{(n-k)e^{s_{k+1}}}{ke^{s_{k}}+(n-k)e^{s_{k+1}}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{k}{\,n-k\,}e^{\Delta_{k}}}.
Proof.

Write Stop=∑j≤kesjS_{\text{top}}=\sum_{j\leq k}e^{s_{j}} and Stail=∑j>kesjS_{\text{tail}}=\sum_{j>k}e^{s_{j}}. Because sj≥sks_{j}\geq s_{k} for j≤kj\leq k and sj≤sk+1s_{j}\leq s_{k+1} for j>kj>k, we have

Stop≥k​esk,Stail≤(n−k)​esk+1.S_{\text{top}}\geq k\,e^{s_{k}},\hskip 20.00003ptS_{\text{tail}}\leq(n-k)\,e^{s_{k+1}}.

Using Lemma A.1, the total-variation error is

TV⁡(P,P^)=StailStop+Stail,\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{S_{\text{tail}}}{S_{\text{top}}+S_{\text{tail}}},

which gives

TV⁡(P,P^)≤(n−k)​esk+1k​esk+(n−k)​esk+1=11+kn−k​eΔk.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\frac{(n-k)e^{s_{k+1}}}{ke^{s_{k}}+(n-k)e^{s_{k+1}}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{k}{\,n-k\,}e^{\Delta_{k}}}.

∎

Remark 4.6.

The bound in Theorem 4.5 is tight in the extremal case where all Top-kk scores equal sks_{k} and all remaining scores equal sk+1s_{k+1}.

Interpretation.

A single large boundary gap Δk\Delta_{k} exponentially suppresses the tail mass. For instance, with n=104n=10^{4} and k=32k=32, to ensure TV≤10−4\operatorname{TV}\leq 10^{-4} one needs Δk≳15\Delta_{k}\gtrsim 15 (by Theorem 4.5). Such a Δk\Delta_{k} ensures that the truncated attention output differs from the full one by less than 0.01%0.01\% in total probability mass.

4.4.2 A Pigeonhole Lemma for Multiple Gaps

For finer control one may use several adjacent score gaps of the ordered list s1≥⋯≥sns_{1}\geq\cdots\geq s_{n}. Define the boundary gaps

Δj:=sj−sj+1(1≤j<n),\Delta_{j}\;:=\;s_{j}-s_{j+1}\hskip 20.00003pt(1\leq j<n),

and the local average of the next m+1m{+}1 gaps past the boundary kk,

Δ¯m+1:=1m+1​∑r=kk+mΔr=sk−sk+m+1m+1.\bar{\Delta}_{m+1}\;:=\;\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{r=k}^{k+m}\Delta_{r}\;=\;\frac{s_{k}-s_{k+m+1}}{m+1}.
Lemma 4.7 (Multi-gap tail split).

Let 1≤k<n1\leq k<n and m≥0m\geq 0 with k+m+1≤nk+m+1\leq n. Then the total-variation error of Top-kk truncation satisfies

TV⁡(P,P^)≤1k​[m​esk+1−sk+(n−k−m)​esk+m+1−sk].\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;\leq\;\frac{1}{k}\Big[\,m\,e^{\,s_{k+1}-s_{k}}\;+\;(n-k-m)\,e^{\,s_{k+m+1}-s_{k}}\Big]. (4.1)

Equivalently, in terms of gaps,

TV⁡(P,P^)≤1k​[m​e−Δk+(n−k−m)​e−(m+1)​Δ¯m+1].\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;\leq\;\frac{1}{k}\Big[\,m\,e^{-\Delta_{k}}\;+\;(n-k-m)\,e^{-(m+1)\bar{\Delta}_{m+1}}\Big]. (4.2)
Proof.

Write Stop=∑j≤kesjS_{\text{top}}=\sum_{j\leq k}e^{s_{j}} and Stail=∑j>kesjS_{\text{tail}}=\sum_{j>k}e^{s_{j}}. Since sj≥sks_{j}\geq s_{k} for j≤kj\leq k, we have Stop≥k​eskS_{\text{top}}\geq k\,e^{s_{k}}.

Split the tail into the first mm discarded entries and the remainder:

Stail=∑j=k+1k+mesj+∑j=k+m+1nesj.S_{\text{tail}}=\!\sum_{j=k+1}^{k+m}e^{s_{j}}\;+\!\sum_{j=k+m+1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}.

By monotonicity, for k+1≤j≤k+mk{+}1\leq j\leq k{+}m we have sj≤sk+1s_{j}\leq s_{k+1}, hence ∑j=k+1k+mesj≤m​esk+1\sum_{j=k+1}^{k+m}e^{s_{j}}\leq m\,e^{s_{k+1}}; and for j≥k+m+1j\geq k{+}m{+}1, sj≤sk+m+1s_{j}\leq s_{k+m+1}, hence ∑j=k+m+1nesj≤(n−k−m)​esk+m+1\sum_{j=k+m+1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}\leq(n-k-m)\,e^{s_{k+m+1}}. Therefore

TV⁡(P,P^)=StailStop+Stail≤StailStop≤m​esk+1+(n−k−m)​esk+m+1k​esk,\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{S_{\text{tail}}}{S_{\text{top}}+S_{\text{tail}}}\leq\frac{S_{\text{tail}}}{S_{\text{top}}}\leq\frac{m\,e^{s_{k+1}}+(n-k-m)\,e^{s_{k+m+1}}}{k\,e^{s_{k}}},

which gives (4.1). Using sk+1−sk=−Δks_{k+1}-s_{k}=-\Delta_{k} and sk+m+1−sk=−∑r=kk+mΔr=−(m+1)Δ¯m+1s_{k+m+1}-s_{k}=-\sum_{r=k}^{k+m}\Delta_{r}=-(m{+}1)\bar{\Delta}_{m+1}, we obtain (4.2). ∎

4.5 Blockwise Deterministic Bounds

When attention is computed in structured partitions—such as heads, local windows, or tiles—it is natural to consider truncation at the block level. Let ℬ={B1,…,BM}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{M}\} be a disjoint partition of indices, and let each block contribute total unnormalized mass

Zj=∑i∈Bjesi,wj=log⁡Zj.Z_{j}=\sum_{i\in B_{j}}e^{s_{i}},\hskip 20.00003ptw_{j}=\log Z_{j}.

We order the block masses in non-increasing order

Z(1)≥Z(2)≥⋯≥Z(M),Z_{(1)}\geq Z_{(2)}\geq\dots\geq Z_{(M)},

and denote by the Top-α\alpha blocks {B(1),…,B(α)}\{B_{(1)},\dots,B_{(\alpha)}\} the kept set after truncation. Let

Zhead:=∑j≤αZ(j),Ztail:=∑j>αZ(j).Z_{\text{head}}:=\sum_{j\leq\alpha}Z_{(j)},\hskip 20.00003ptZ_{\text{tail}}:=\sum_{j>\alpha}Z_{(j)}.

The overall total variation error equals the normalized tail mass,

TV(P,P^)=ZtailZhead+Ztail=∑i∉∪j≤αB(j)pi,pi=esi∑kesk.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{tail}}}{Z_{\mathrm{head}}+Z_{\mathrm{tail}}}=\sum_{i\notin\cup_{j\leq\alpha}B_{(j)}}p_{i},\hskip 20.00003ptp_{i}=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{\sum_{k}e^{s_{k}}}.
Gap–based bound (sharper form).

For an integer 1≤α<M1\leq\alpha<M, let the inter-block gap be

Δblk=w(α)−w(α+1)=log⁡Z(α)Z(α+1).\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}=w_{(\alpha)}-w_{(\alpha+1)}=\log\!\frac{Z_{(\alpha)}}{Z_{(\alpha+1)}}.

Then

TV⁡(P,P^)≤1 1+αM−α​eΔblk≤M−αα​e−Δblk.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\,1+\dfrac{\alpha}{M-\alpha}\,e^{\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}}\,}\;\leq\;\frac{M-\alpha}{\alpha}\,e^{-\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}}. (4.3)

Proof. Using Zhead≥α​Z(α)Z_{\text{head}}\!\geq\!\alpha Z_{(\alpha)} and Ztail≤(M−α)​Z(α+1)Z_{\text{tail}}\!\leq\!(M-\alpha)Z_{(\alpha+1)},

TV⁡(P,P^)=ZtailZhead+Ztail=11+Zhead/Ztail≤11+αM−α​Z(α)Z(α+1)=11+αM−α​eΔblk.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{Z_{\text{tail}}}{Z_{\text{head}}+Z_{\text{tail}}}\ =\frac{1}{1+Z_{\text{head}}/Z_{\text{tail}}}\leq\frac{1}{1+\frac{\alpha}{M-\alpha}\frac{Z_{(\alpha)}}{Z_{(\alpha+1)}}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\alpha}{M-\alpha}e^{\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}}}.
Existence of a sufficient gap.

Among the MM ordered block masses, there always exists at least one pair of adjacent blocks satisfying

w(j)−w(j+1)≥w(1)−w(M)M−1,w_{(j)}-w_{(j+1)}\geq\frac{w_{(1)}-w_{(M)}}{M-1},

since ∑j=1M−1(w(j)−w(j+1))=w(1)−w(M).\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\bigl(w_{(j)}-w_{(j+1)}\bigr)=w_{(1)}-w_{(M)}. Thus, in practice even modest variations in block mass typically produce a nontrivial certified gap.

Discussion.

Equation (4.3) provides a simple, fully verifiable certificate for structured sparsification: keeping the top-α\alpha blocks guarantees that the total variation error is bounded by 1/(1+αM−α​eΔblk)1\big/\!\big(1+\tfrac{\alpha}{M-\alpha}e^{\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}}\big) (and hence by (M−α)/α⋅e−Δblk(M-\alpha)/\alpha\cdot e^{-\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}}}). This bound depends only on observable block statistics and requires no probabilistic assumptions. In implementation, Δblk\Delta_{\mathrm{blk}} can be estimated from a small subset of scores using inexpensive upper bounds, enabling efficient certified pruning across heads or local windows.

4.6 Blockwise Mass-Certificate Bounds

While the gap-based bound of Section 4.5 relies on a single inter-block gap Δblk\Delta_{\text{blk}}, it may be conservative when several near-top blocks share similar mass. A more adaptive approach is to certify directly on blockwise sums, in analogy to the Mass-Certificate Search (MC-Search) of Section 7.2. Here, the goal is to verify that the retained set of α\alpha blocks captures a sufficient fraction of the total mass, even when block gaps are small.

Setup.

Let ℬ={B1,…,BM}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{M}\} be a disjoint block partition with block masses Zb=∑i∈BbesiZ_{b}=\sum_{i\in B_{b}}e^{s_{i}} and block probabilities pb=Zb/∑r=1MZrp_{b}=Z_{b}/\sum_{r=1}^{M}Z_{r}. For any candidate kept set K⊆{1,…,M}K\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\} with |K|=α|K|=\alpha, the total-variation error equals the normalized tail mass,

TV⁡(P,P^)=StailShead+Stail,Shead=∑b∈KZb,Stail=∑b∉KZb.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\,=\,\frac{S_{\text{tail}}}{S_{\text{head}}+S_{\text{tail}}},\hskip 20.00003ptS_{\text{head}}=\sum_{b\in K}Z_{b},\hskip 10.00002ptS_{\text{tail}}=\sum_{b\notin K}Z_{b}.

In practice, the exact ZbZ_{b} may be unavailable, but can be bounded via partial scoring or block-level upper/lower estimates.

Mass-certificate bound.

Suppose each block bb has known lower and upper bounds Lb≤Zb≤UbL_{b}\leq Z_{b}\leq U_{b}. Let Kα​(L)K_{\alpha}(L) denote the α\alpha blocks with the largest lower bounds LbL_{b} (this choice maximizes the kept-mass lower bound). Then an upper bound on the total-variation error for the specific kept set Kα​(L)K_{\alpha}(L), consistent with these bounds, is

TV⁡(P,P^)≤S+​(U)S−​(L)+S+​(U),S−​(L)=∑b∈Kα​(L)Lb,S+​(U)=∑b∉Kα​(L)Ub.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;\leq\;\frac{S^{+}(U)}{S^{-}(L)+S^{+}(U)},\hskip 20.00003ptS^{-}(L)=\sum_{b\in K_{\alpha}(L)}L_{b},\hskip 10.00002ptS^{+}(U)=\sum_{b\notin K_{\alpha}(L)}U_{b}. (4.4)

This bound is deterministic and verifiable: if the right-hand side is below ε\varepsilon, the corresponding block set Kα​(L)K_{\alpha}(L) is guaranteed to satisfy TV≤ε\operatorname{TV}\leq\varepsilon for all realizations of the true block masses.

Interpretation.

Equation (4.4) is the blockwise analogue of the tokenwise MC-certificate of Section 7 . The quantity S−​(L)S^{-}(L) is a conservative underestimate of the kept-block mass, while S+​(U)S^{+}(U) is a conservative overestimate of the discarded-block mass. Their ratio yields a provable upper bound on the tail probability fraction,

TV≤S+​(U)S−​(L)+S+​(U)=1 1+S−​(L)S+​(U).\operatorname{TV}\;\leq\;\frac{S^{+}(U)}{S^{-}(L)+S^{+}(U)}\,=\,\frac{1}{\,1+\dfrac{S^{-}(L)}{S^{+}(U)}\,}.

Because both LbL_{b} and UbU_{b} tighten monotonically as more tokens are scored, the bound improves adaptively and converges to equality once all blocks are fully evaluated.

Transition to Output Bounds. The results in this section provide a hierarchy of distribution-level certificates: exact identities in TV and KL, pointwise and multi-gap bounds, and blockwise gap- and mass-based bounds. In the next section we show how these certified deviations in TV⁡(P,P^)\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P}) translate into guarantees on the actual attention outputs, yielding tight ℓ2\ell_{2} error bounds that explicitly incorporate the geometry of the value matrix VV.

5 Output-Level Error Bounds and Geometry of the Value Matrix

Having established distribution-level control via total variation and KL, we now quantify how Top-kk truncation affects the actual attention outputs. We first convert TV bounds into basic ℓ2\ell_{2} guarantees, then refine them using an exact head–tail decomposition, geometric (diameter) and variance-based bounds, and finally formulate a graph-theoretic problem that characterizes the optimal head–tail partition.

5.1 Basic ℓ2\ell_{2} Bounds via Total Variation

The TV distance bounds derived in the previous section directly translate into Euclidean errors on the resulting attention outputs.

Proposition 5.1 (Output error).

Let V∈ℝn×dvV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{v}} and assume ‖vj‖2≤C\|v_{j}\|_{2}\leq C for all rows vjv_{j}. Then

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤2​C​TV⁡(P,P^).\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\leq 2C\,\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P}).
Proof.

See Appendix A.4. ∎

This provides a certified ℓ2\ell_{2} guarantee on the attention outputs: once a sufficient score gap is observed, the truncation error on the resulting value vector is bounded by 2​C2C times the small total-variation mass.

5.2 Exact Head–Tail Decomposition

We next refine this crude bound by expressing the output error exactly in terms of conditional means over the retained and discarded sets.

Theorem 5.2 (Exact head–tail identity).

Let P=(pi)i=1nP=(p_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be the attention weights and P^=(p^i)\widehat{P}=(\widehat{p}_{i}) their Top-kk truncation. Let τ:=∑i>kpi\tau:=\sum_{i>k}p_{i} denote the tail mass and define the conditional means

μhead:=∑i≤kpi​vi1−τ,μtail:=∑i>kpi​viτ(μtail=0 if τ=0).\mu_{\mathrm{head}}:=\frac{\sum_{i\leq k}p_{i}v_{i}}{1-\tau},\hskip 20.00003pt\mu_{\mathrm{tail}}:=\frac{\sum_{i>k}p_{i}v_{i}}{\tau}\hskip 10.00002pt(\mu_{\mathrm{tail}}=0\text{ if }\tau=0).

Then the exact identity

Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)=τ⁡(μtail−μhead)\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)=\tau\,(\mu_{\mathrm{tail}}-\mu_{\mathrm{head}})

holds, so that

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2=τ​‖μtail−μhead‖2.\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}=\tau\,\|\mu_{\mathrm{tail}}-\mu_{\mathrm{head}}\|_{2}.

(Proof in Appendix A.4.)

5.3 Head–Tail Diameter Bound

The exact decomposition suggests a geometric control of the error via the spread of the value vectors across the head–tail cut.

Proposition 5.3 (Head–tail diameter bound).

Define the cross–set diameter

diamH,T:=maxi>kj≤k⁡‖vi−vj‖2.\mathrm{diam}_{H,T}:=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}i>k\\ j\leq k\end{subarray}}\|v_{i}-v_{j}\|_{2}.

Then

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤τ​diamH,T.\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\leq\tau\,\mathrm{diam}_{H,T}.

If ‖vi‖≤C\|v_{i}\|\leq C for all ii, then diamH,T≤2​C\mathrm{diam}_{H,T}\leq 2C, recovering the classical 2​C​τ2C\tau bound as a special case. (Proof in Appendix A.5.)

5.4 Variance-Based Bounds

We now complement the diameter bound with variance-based control that explicitly involves the value variance under the full attention distribution.

Proposition 5.4 (Centered χ2\chi^{2}–variance bound).

Let μP:=∑ipi​vi\mu_{P}:=\sum_{i}p_{i}v_{i} and define the value variance under PP by

VarP⁡(V):=∑i=1npi​‖vi−μP‖22.\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\|v_{i}-\mu_{P}\|_{2}^{2}.

Then

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤Dχ2(P^∥P)​VarP⁡(V),\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{D_{\chi^{2}}(\widehat{P}\|P)}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V)},

and for Top-kk truncation Dχ2(P^∥P)=τ/(1−τ)D_{\chi^{2}}(\widehat{P}\|P)=\tau/(1-\tau). (Proof in Appendix A.6.)

Corollary 5.5 (Centered KL–variance bound).

Since KL(P^∥P)=−log(1−τ)\mathrm{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)=-\log(1-\tau) for Top-kk,

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤eKL(P^∥P)−1​VarP⁡(V).\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{e^{\mathrm{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)}-1}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V)}.

(Proof in Appendix A.6.)

5.5 Combined “Best Available” Certificate

Finally, we collect the preceding bounds into a single inequality that automatically chooses the sharpest available guarantee for a given configuration of PP and VV.

Theorem 5.6 (Best available certificate).

Let C≥maxi⁡‖vi‖2C\geq\max_{i}\|v_{i}\|_{2}. For Top-kk truncation,

‖Attn⁡(q,K,V)−Attnk⁡(q,K,V)‖2≤min⁡{τ​diamH,T,Dχ2(P^∥P)​VarP⁡(V), 2​C​τ}.\boxed{\bigl\|\operatorname{Attn}(q,K,V)-\operatorname{Attn}_{k}(q,K,V)\bigr\|_{2}\leq\min\!\Bigl\{\tau\,\mathrm{diam}_{H,T},\;\sqrt{D_{\chi^{2}}(\widehat{P}\|P)}\,\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V)},\;2C\tau\Bigr\}.}

This bound never exceeds 2​C​τ2C\tau, and it is strictly smaller whenever at least one of the diameter or variance terms is less than 2​C​τ2C\tau (for example, whenever diamH,T<2​C\mathrm{diam}_{H,T}<2C or when VarP⁡(V)\operatorname{Var}_{P}(V) is substantially smaller than C2C^{2}). (Proof in  A.10)

Proposition 5.3 introduces a new combinatorial optimization problem: given the value vectors {vi}\{v_{i}\}, how should we choose the head set to minimize the cross-set diameter?

5.6 Graph-Theoretic Optimization of the Head–Tail Diameter

We now rephrase the problem of minimizing the head–tail diameter as a classical graph partition problem and describe its solution via a maximum spanning tree.

5.6.1 Problem statement

Let 𝒱={1,…,n}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,n\} be nn items (points), and let wi​j=wj​i≥0w_{ij}=w_{ji}\geq 0 be the weight of edge {i,j}\{i,j\} (e.g. the Euclidean distance ‖vi−vj‖2\|v_{i}-v_{j}\|_{2}). For any non-empty proper subset H⊂𝒱H\subset\mathcal{V} (i.e., 1≤|H|≤n−11\leq|H|\leq n-1), define the cut value

ϕ(H):=max{wi​j:i∈H,j∈𝒱∖H}.\phi(H)\;:=\;\max\{\,w_{ij}:\;i\in H,\;j\in\mathcal{V}\setminus H\,\}.

Our goal is the ""minimax"" problem

ϕ⋆=minH⊂𝒱, 1≤|H|≤n−1⁡ϕ⁡(H)\boxed{\hskip 10.00002pt\phi^{\star}\;=\;\min_{H\subset\mathcal{V},\;1\leq|H|\leq n-1}\;\phi(H)\hskip 10.00002pt}

and an optimal partition achieving it.

One-line summary (what we will prove).

Compute a maximum spanning tree (MaxST) and delete its lightest edge; the two components form an optimal cut and the weight of that deleted edge equals ϕ⋆\phi^{\star}.

5.6.2 A threshold view of the problem

For a real number τ\tau, let G>τG_{>\tau} be the graph on 𝒱\mathcal{V} that keeps exactly those edges whose weight is strictly greater than τ\tau.

Lemma 5.7 (Feasibility via disconnection).

There exists a non-trivial HH with ϕ⁡(H)≤τ\phi(H)\leq\tau if and only if G>τG_{>\tau} is disconnected.

Proof.

If G>τG_{>\tau} is disconnected, take HH to be a union of its connected components; then every edge crossing the cut has weight ≤τ\leq\tau. Conversely, if G>τG_{>\tau} is connected, any bipartition must cut some edge of G>τG_{>\tau}, so its largest cross edge >τ>\tau. ∎

By Lemma 5.7, ϕ⋆\phi^{\star} is the smallest τ\tau for which G>τG_{>\tau} becomes disconnected.

5.6.3 Maximum spanning tree characterization

A maximum spanning tree (MaxST) is a spanning tree whose total weight is maximal. Let T⋆T^{\star} be any MaxST, and let

α:=min⁡{we:e∈T⋆}\alpha\;:=\;\min\{\,w_{e}:\;e\in T^{\star}\,\}

be the weight of its lightest edge.

Theorem 5.8 (Main theorem).

ϕ⋆=α\phi^{\star}=\alpha. Moreover, deleting from T⋆T^{\star} any lightest edge splits 𝒱\mathcal{V} into two parts (H,𝒱∖H)(H,\mathcal{V}\setminus H) with ϕ⁡(H)=α\phi(H)=\alpha, hence (H,𝒱∖H)(H,\mathcal{V}\setminus H) is an optimal cut. Conversely, every optimal cut is a union of connected components of G>αG_{>\alpha}.

Proof.

Run Kruskal in descending order (or negate weights and run standard Kruskal). Let emine_{\min} be the last edge Kruskal adds to complete a spanning tree; its weight is α\alpha. Right before adding emine_{\min}, Kruskal has examined all edges >α>\alpha and the graph is still disconnected, so G>αG_{>\alpha} is disconnected. For any τ<α\tau<\alpha Kruskal already has a spanning tree using only edges >τ>\tau, hence G>τG_{>\tau} is connected. Therefore the first threshold where connectivity breaks is exactly α\alpha, i.e., ϕ⋆=α\phi^{\star}=\alpha by Lemma 5.7. Removing emine_{\min} gives a cut whose cross edges are all ≤α\leq\alpha, and since emine_{\min} itself crosses this cut with weight α\alpha, we have ϕ⁡(H)=α\phi(H)=\alpha; optimality follows since no cut can get below α\alpha. ∎

Tie handling.

If multiple edges have weight α\alpha, G>αG_{>\alpha} may have more than two components. Any non-empty union of these components is optimal and attains value α\alpha.

5.6.4 Algorithms (easy to implement)

Kruskal (descending order).
  1. 1.

    Build the edge list (i,j,wi​j)(i,j,w_{ij}) and sort it by wi​jw_{ij} in descending order (breaking ties arbitrarily).

  2. 2.

    Maintain a disjoint-set union (union–find) structure. Scan edges in order and add (i,j)(i,j) if and only if it connects two different components.

  3. 3.

    Stop when a single connected component remains (equivalently, after adding n−1n-1 edges in a complete graph). The resulting tree is a MaxST. The lightest selected edge has weight α\alpha and is the one to cut.

Cost. Sorting dominates: O⁡(m​log⁡m)O(m\log m) time for mm edges (plus near-linear union–find time). For a complete graph, m=(n2)m=\binom{n}{2}, so the total cost is O⁡(n2​log⁡n)O(n^{2}\log n).

6 Probabilistic Analysis under a Gaussian Score Model

The deterministic results of Section 4 apply to any finite set of scores. To understand how large the Top-kk set must be, on average, to ensure a given error tolerance ε\varepsilon, we now adopt a simple but analytically tractable probabilistic model for the scores. Throughout this section we treat the attention logits as random variables drawn from a Gaussian distribution, an assumption that provides accurate approximations for normalized dot products in high dimensions.

6.1 Setup and Notation

Let the normalized scores be i.i.d.

si∼𝒩(μ,σ2),i=1,…,n.s_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}),\hskip 20.00003pti=1,\dots,n.

Define the exponential weights wi=esiw_{i}=e^{s_{i}} and note that 𝔼⁡[wi]=eμ+σ2/2\mathbb{E}[w_{i}]=e^{\mu+\sigma^{2}/2}. The softmax normalization for one query is

Zn=∑i=1nwi,pi=wiZn.Z_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i},\hskip 20.00003ptp_{i}=\frac{w_{i}}{Z_{n}}.

For a threshold tt, denote the tail mass (fraction of the softmax weight above tt) by

τn(t)=∑i:si>twi∑i=1nwi.\tau_{n}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i:s_{i}>t}w_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}}. (6.1)

Truncating at the kk-th largest score corresponds to choosing a random threshold TkT_{k} satisfying #⁡{i:si>Tk}=k\#\{i:s_{i}>T_{k}\}=k, and the resulting total variation error equals τn​(Tk)\tau_{n}(T_{k}).

All Gaussian-moment formulas used in this subsection (e.g., 𝔼⁡[wi]=eμ+σ2/2\mathbb{E}[w_{i}]=e^{\mu+\sigma^{2}/2}) are derived in Appendix B.

6.2 Law of Large Numbers for Exponential Weights

By the strong law of large numbers,

1n∑i=1nwi→a.s.𝔼[wi]=eμ+σ2/2,1n∑i=1nwi 1{si>t}→a.s.𝔼[wi 1{si>t}].\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;\mathbb{E}[w_{i}]=e^{\mu+\sigma^{2}/2},\hskip 20.00003pt\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{s_{i}>t\}}\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;\mathbb{E}[w_{i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{s_{i}>t\}}].

Using the log-normal moment identity, we obtain

𝔼[wi 1{si>t}]=eμ+σ2/2Φc(t−μ−σ2σ),\mathbb{E}[w_{i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{s_{i}>t\}}]=e^{\mu+\sigma^{2}/2}\,\Phi_{c}\!\left(\frac{t-\mu-\sigma^{2}}{\sigma}\right),

where Φc​(x)=1−Φ⁡(x)\Phi_{c}(x)=1-\Phi(x) is the Gaussian survival function. Therefore, by the continuous mapping theorem,

τn(t)=∑i:si>twi∑i=1nwi→a.s.Φc(t−μ−σ2σ).\tau_{n}(t)=\frac{\sum_{i:s_{i}>t}w_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}}\;\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\;\Phi_{c}\!\left(\frac{t-\mu-\sigma^{2}}{\sigma}\right). (6.2)

Equation (6.2) states that the softmax tail mass converges almost surely to a deterministic function of tt, μ\mu, and σ\sigma. A detailed derivation of the log-normal moment identity and the limit (6.2) is given in Appendix B.

6.3 Asymptotic Threshold for a Target Error

Let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) be a desired bound on the total-variation error. Define the asymptotic threshold tεt_{\varepsilon} by

Φc​(tε−μ−σ2σ)=1−ε.\Phi_{c}\!\left(\frac{t_{\varepsilon}-\mu-\sigma^{2}}{\sigma}\right)=1-\varepsilon.

Solving for tεt_{\varepsilon} gives

tε=μ+σ2+σ​Φ−1​(ε),t_{\varepsilon}=\mu+\sigma^{2}+\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon), (6.3)

where Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is the quantile function of the standard normal. This threshold separates the top ε\varepsilon fraction of exponential weight from the remainder in expectation.

The expected Top-kk size achieving error ε\varepsilon is therefore

kε≈n​Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(ε)).k_{\varepsilon}\;\approx\;n\,\Phi_{c}\!\bigl(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)\bigr). (6.4)

6.4 Implications

Equations (6.3)–(6.4) provide a closed-form mapping between the desired truncation error ε\varepsilon, the score variance σ2\sigma^{2}, and the expected fraction k/nk/n of keys to keep. For moderate σ\sigma, the relation is nearly linear on a log–probability scale, consistent with empirical fits observed in simulation. Combined with the deterministic bounds from Section 4, these results allow one to design Top-kk attention mechanisms that achieve provable accuracy guarantees with predictable sparsity.

6.5 Empirical Verification of the Gaussian Law

In Section 6.3 we derived the asymptotic law that the expected Top-kk size achieving error ε\varepsilon under the Gaussian score model satisfies

kε≈n​Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(1−ε)).k_{\varepsilon}\;\approx\;n\,\Phi_{c}\!\bigl(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\bigr).

For convenience, we denote this prediction by

αGauss​(ε,σ):=n​Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(1−ε)),\alpha_{\text{Gauss}}(\varepsilon,\sigma):=n\,\Phi_{c}\!\bigl(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\bigr),

which predicts the expected Top-kk size (or equivalently, the effective sparsity level) required to ensure a prescribed total-variation error ε\varepsilon under a Gaussian score model.

Experimental question.

We now test the quantitative accuracy of this law in practice. Specifically, we ask:

For which values of the score variance σ\sigma does our Gaussian approximation remain accurate?

Setup.

We generated independent Gaussian scores si∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)s_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) for n=10,000n=10{,}000 and computed the empirical value of αemp\alpha_{\text{emp}}, the minimal number of retained keys ensuring TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\mathrm{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon, over 10001000 Monte Carlo repetitions. We then compared αemp\alpha_{\text{emp}} with the theoretical prediction αGauss​(ε,σ)\alpha_{\text{Gauss}}(\varepsilon,\sigma) for ε∈{10−3, 5×10−3, 10−2}\varepsilon\in\{10^{-3},\,5\times 10^{-3},\,10^{-2}\} and σ\sigma spanning [0.1,3.0][0.1,3.0].

Results.

Table 2 reports both theoretical and empirical values. Across all regimes tested, the two agree to within numerical precision: for σ≤3\sigma\!\leq\!3, the relative deviation |αemp−αGauss|/αGauss|\alpha_{\text{emp}}-\alpha_{\text{Gauss}}|/\alpha_{\text{Gauss}} remains below 0.1%0.1\%. Figure 1 visualizes this near-perfect alignment. Surprisingly, the Gaussian formula remains extremely accurate even for moderate σ\sigma where the log-normal tail approximation could have broken down.

Takeaway.

The empirical agreement confirms that the probabilistic law derived in Section 6 provides a quantitatively precise description of the softmax tail mass. For all practical regimes of interest (σ≲3\sigma\lesssim 3), the Gaussian prediction can be used as a direct design rule linking sparsity, variance, and target accuracy.

7 Certifying Selection Algorithms for Top-kk Truncation

The deterministic and probabilistic results derived above yield explicit conditions under which a Top-kk approximation achieves a prescribed total-variation error ε\varepsilon. In this section we translate those conditions into concrete certifying algorithms that identify the required subset of keys without exhaustively computing all nn scores.

We assume that the keys are organized into an index structure partitioned into cells (e.g., tiles or clusters) with precomputed centers cjc_{j} and radii rjr_{j}, so that each cell admits an upper bound Uj​(q)U_{j}(q) on the dot products q⋅kq\!\cdot\!k for keys it contains. Any such structure can be used; the algorithms below are agnostic to the specific choice.

7.1 Δk\Delta_{k}-Search: Gap-Based Certification

Intuition.

From Theorem 4.5, the truncation error obeys the sharp inequality

TV⁡(P,P^)≤11+kn−k​eΔk,Δk=sk−sk+1.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\;\leq\;\frac{1}{1+\tfrac{k}{n-k}e^{\Delta_{k}}},\hskip 20.00003pt\Delta_{k}=s_{k}-s_{k+1}.

Thus, to guarantee TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon, it suffices that

Δk≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε.\Delta_{k}\;\geq\;\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}\;+\;\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.

The idea of Δk\Delta_{k}-Search is to explore the key space progressively until this inequality is certified without scoring all items.

Theorem 7.1 (Correctness of Δk\Delta_{k}-Search).

Whenever Algorithm 1 terminates, the returned set ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} satisfies TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon.

Sketch.

If Lk−Uout≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εεL_{k}-U_{\text{out}}\geq\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}, then for all unscored keys jj,

sj≤Uout≤sk−[log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε],s_{j}\leq U_{\text{out}}\leq s_{k}-\Big[\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Big],

so that Δk≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε\Delta_{k}\geq\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}. Applying Theorem 4.5 yields TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon. ∎

Complexity.

Δk\Delta_{k}-Search terminates after scoring only keys contained in cells whose upper bounds exceed

Lk−[log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε].L_{k}-\Big[\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\Big].

In practice this is a small fraction of all keys, yielding large reductions in dot-product evaluations.

7.2 MC-Search: Sum-Wise Mass Certification

Intuition.

While Δk\Delta_{k}-Search relies on a single boundary gap, it may be conservative when several near-top keys have similar scores. Mass-Certificate Search (MC-Search) exploits the exact tail–mass identity

TV⁡(P,P^)=StailShead+Stail,\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{S_{\text{tail}}}{S_{\text{head}}+S_{\text{tail}}},

and certifies TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon by upper-bounding the unscored exponential tail mass.

Let SS be the set of evaluated keys and let ℐk⊆S\mathcal{I}_{k}\subseteq S be the current candidate Top-kk among the evaluated keys. Define

Sheadknown=∑i∈ℐkesi,Stailknown=∑i∈S∖ℐkesi.S_{\text{head}}^{\text{known}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}e^{s_{i}},\hskip 20.00003ptS_{\text{tail}}^{\text{known}}=\sum_{i\in S\setminus\mathcal{I}_{k}}e^{s_{i}}.

For each unexplored cell jj, let Uj​(q)U_{j}(q) be an upper bound on q⋅kq\!\cdot\!k over that cell, and let 𝒰\mathcal{U} denote the set of unexplored cells. The algorithm maintains the running upper estimate

τ^k=Stailknown+∑j∈𝒰eUj​(q)Sheadknown+Stailknown.\widehat{\tau}_{k}=\frac{\,S_{\text{tail}}^{\text{known}}+\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}}e^{U_{j}(q)}\,}{\,S_{\text{head}}^{\text{known}}+S_{\text{tail}}^{\text{known}}\,}.

If τ^k≤ε\widehat{\tau}_{k}\leq\varepsilon, the certificate TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon is proven.

Theorem 7.2 (Correctness of MC-Search).

If Algorithm 2 terminates, then the resulting set ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} satisfies TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon.

Sketch.

By construction, for all unscored keys jj we have sj≤Uj​(q)s_{j}\leq U_{j}(q); hence the true tail mass is at most Stailknown+∑j∈𝒰eUj​(q)S_{\text{tail}}^{\text{known}}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{U}}e^{U_{j}(q)}, while the total mass is at least Sheadknown+StailknownS_{\text{head}}^{\text{known}}+S_{\text{tail}}^{\text{known}}. Therefore TV⁡(P,P^)≤τ^k\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\widehat{\tau}_{k}, and if τ^k≤ε\widehat{\tau}_{k}\leq\varepsilon upon termination, then TV⁡(P,P^)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})\leq\varepsilon (by the tail–mass identity, Lemma A.1). ∎

Complexity.

MC-Search can adaptively focus on high-probability cells and may terminate earlier than Δk\Delta_{k}-Search when the tail distribution is flat, at the cost of slightly more bookkeeping. Both algorithms share O⁡(k​log⁡n)O(k\log n) memory and sublinear scoring behavior in typical regimes.

7.3 Comparative Discussion

The two certified algorithms instantiate distinct philosophies:

  • •

    Δk\Delta_{k}-Search uses a local certificate (a single gap) and excels when score distributions exhibit clear separations between relevant and irrelevant keys.

  • •

    MC-Search relies on a global mass certificate, advantageous when many keys have similar scores or when hierarchical index structures provide tight cell bounds.

In practice they can be combined: a fast Δk\Delta_{k}-Search pass first certifies most queries, while difficult cases fall back to MC-Search. Both algorithms translate the mathematical conditions of Sections 4–6 into implementable selection procedures with provable accuracy guarantees.

8 Empirical Validation on Real Attention Maps

We now test the theory and certified algorithms on both real attention maps from bert-base-uncased and controlled synthetic settings. This section focuses on how often Top-kk truncation meets a target TV tolerance, how aggressive certified sparsity can be in practice, and how these behaviors scale with sequence length and tolerance.

Setup.

We evaluate the proposed certificates on bert-base-uncased using real attention probabilities returned by the model (output_attentions=True). Inputs are longer paragraphs (tokenized to average length n¯≈15\bar{n}\approx 15 in this run). Unless otherwise stated, we target an error tolerance ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01 and request a nominal k=16k=16, but enforce query-wise kadj=min⁡(k,n−1)k_{\mathrm{adj}}=\min(k,n-1) so that truncation is non-trivial for n≤kn\leq k. We collect per-query (layer, head, position) statistics over 6,0486{,}048 attention distributions.

8.1 Results on BERT Attention

Aggregate behavior.

Across 6,0486{,}048 queries (mean length n¯=15.0\bar{n}=15.0), the requested k=16k=16 becomes k¯adj=13.10\bar{k}_{\mathrm{adj}}=13.10. The observed truncation error (exact tail mass) has

TVmean=0.00782<ε,TVmedian=0.00330,TV95%=0.0301.\mathrm{TV}_{\text{mean}}=0.00782<\varepsilon,\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{TV}_{\text{median}}=0.00330,\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{TV}_{95\%}=0.0301.

Thus, while the average query is within tolerance, about 5%5\% of queries exceed ε\varepsilon under a fixed-kk policy.

Gap certificate (local Δ\Delta).

The deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate passes on only 1.79%1.79\% of queries overall. This is consistent with the threshold

Δ≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε≈log⁡(213⋅0.990.01)≈2.73,\Delta\;\geq\;\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\approx\log\!\Bigl(\frac{2}{13}\cdot\frac{0.99}{0.01}\Bigr)\approx 2.73,

(using representative (n,k)=(15,13)(n,k)=(15,13)), whereas the empirical boundary gaps are smaller (overall Δmean=0.489\Delta_{\text{mean}}=0.489, median 0.2970.297). In words: many heads are relatively flat around the kk-boundary, so a single-gap certificate is conservative.

Mass certificate (MC-Search style).

For each query we compute the minimal kmck_{\text{mc}} such that the discarded mass is ≤ε\leq\varepsilon. We obtain

k¯mc=10.95,mean speedup 𝔼[n/kmc]=1.75×.\bar{k}_{\text{mc}}=10.95,\hskip 20.00003pt\text{mean speedup }\mathbb{E}[n/k_{\text{mc}}]=1.75\times.

Hence an adaptive, mass-certified policy attains guaranteed accuracy with materially fewer keys than dense attention on average, and fewer than the fixed kadjk_{\mathrm{adj}}.

Head-wise heterogeneity.

There is substantial variation across heads. Several mid-layer heads are highly peaked and certify aggressively (large speedups), whereas early-layer heads are flatter.

Takeaways.

(i) A fixed-kk setting with k≈13k\approx 13 achieves TVmean<ε\mathrm{TV}_{\text{mean}}<\varepsilon but leaves a non-negligible tail risk (TV95%>ε\mathrm{TV}_{95\%}>\varepsilon). (ii) The mass certificate removes this tail risk by adapting kk per query; it yields ∼1.75×\sim\!1.75\times mean reduction in scored keys overall and up to ∼14×\sim\!14\times in peaked heads. (iii) The Δ\Delta certificate is highly effective in peaked regimes (where a single boundary gap is informative) and conservative in flat regimes; it is therefore best used as a fast first-line check.

8.2 Operating Policies and Certified Efficiency

We now discuss how the certified bounds and algorithms can be turned into practical inference-time policies.

Hybrid (Δ\Delta+MC) policy.

A practical strategy is: (1) attempt Δ\Delta-Search; if

Δ≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε,\Delta\;\geq\;\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon},

stop (certificate passes). (2) Otherwise, invoke MC-Search to raise kk minimally until the empirical tail mass is ≤ε\leq\varepsilon. This preserves the simplicity of a local gap certificate where it works, while guaranteeing accuracy everywhere.

Quantile-based fixed-kk.

If per-query adaptivity is undesirable at inference time, compute the empirical distribution of kmck_{\text{mc}} per layer/head and choose kk as a high quantile (e.g., 9595th) to reduce tail risk while retaining most of the efficiency. Table 3 suggests that per-head quantiles could substantially shrink compute in mid layers without hurting certification.

Scaling with sequence length.

For heads whose distributions remain peaked as nn grows, the expected certified complexity follows O⁡(kmc​d)O(k_{\text{mc}}\,d) with empirical speedups ∝n/kmc\propto n/k_{\text{mc}}. The observed cases with kmc≈−2k_{\text{mc}}\approx 1\!-\!2 indicate large potential gains at longer nn.

8.3 Discussion

These findings mirror the theoretical picture:

  • •

    The deterministic gap bound TV≤n−kk​e−Δ\mathrm{TV}\leq\tfrac{n-k}{k}e^{-\Delta} is sharp when a clear boundary separation exists (large Δ\Delta), hence the strong certification in L2–H0/H9.

  • •

    The mass identity TV=tail mass\mathrm{TV}=\text{tail mass} directly enables certified minimal-kk selection (MC-Search), eliminating violations by construction.

  • •

    Empirically, early heads tend to be flatter (small Δ\Delta; larger kmck_{\text{mc}}), while certain mid-layer heads concentrate mass sharply (small kmck_{\text{mc}}).

Overall, certified Top-kk on real attention maps is both accurate (no bound violations with MC) and efficient (material key reductions), and the hybrid policy operationalizes the theory with minimal overhead.

8.4 Reporting Summary for This Run

For completeness, we summarize the main statistics from the paragraph-length BERT run:

  • •

    Queries analyzed: 6,0486{,}048; mean sequence length n¯=15.0\bar{n}=15.0.

  • •

    Requested k=16k=16; applied kadj=min⁡(k,n−1)k_{\mathrm{adj}}=\min(k,n{-}1); resulting k¯adj=13.10\bar{k}_{\mathrm{adj}}=13.10.

  • •

    Error metrics at kadjk_{\mathrm{adj}}: TVmean=0.00782\mathrm{TV}_{\text{mean}}=0.00782, TVmedian=0.00330\mathrm{TV}_{\text{median}}=0.00330, TV95%=0.0301\mathrm{TV}_{95\%}=0.0301.

  • •

    Gap certificate pass rate: 1.79%1.79\% overall; peaked heads up to 35.7%35.7\%.

  • •

    Mass certificate: k¯mc=10.95\bar{k}_{\text{mc}}=10.95; mean speedup 𝔼[n/kmc]=1.75×\mathbb{E}[n/k_{\text{mc}}]=1.75\times; selected heads up to ∼14×\sim\!14\times.

8.5 Scaling with Sequence Length

We next move from short paragraphs to longer fixed-length windows to examine the effect of sequence length on certified Top-kk.

Setup.

To examine asymptotic behavior, we varied the sequence length of BERT attention from n=128n=128 to 512512 while fixing the requested Top-k=16k=16 and target tolerance ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01. For each length, we evaluated both the deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate and the mass certificate (MC-Search) on all query distributions of bert-base-uncased. The experiment produced between 5.5×1045.5\times 10^{4} and 2.2×1052.2\times 10^{5} query instances per setting.

Observed trends.

As shown in Table 4, the average total-variation error under a fixed-kk truncation increases monotonically with context size:

TVmean=0.160→ 0.208→ 0.263for ​n=128,256,512.\mathrm{TV}_{\text{mean}}=0.160\;\to\;0.208\;\to\;0.263\hskip 10.00002pt\text{for }n=128,256,512.

The 9595th-percentile error rises above 0.50.5, indicating that fixed-kk policies violate the target bound ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01 for a non-negligible fraction of queries. This confirms the theoretically predicted growth of the discarded tail mass with nn when kk is held constant.

Gap vs. Mass certificates.

The deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate required gaps of

Δ≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε≈ 6.5​–​8.0\Delta\;\geq\;\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\;\approx\;6.5\text{--}8.0

for these lengths, whereas empirical gaps were small (Δ¯≈0.07\bar{\Delta}\!\approx\!0.07–0.090.09). Consequently, no query satisfied the Δ\Delta criterion (0%0\% pass rate), illustrating its conservative nature for flat attention distributions. In contrast, the MC-Search certificate—which adaptively increases kk until TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon—identified the minimal certified sizes

k¯mc=59.6, 108.2, 206.2⇒k¯mcn≈0.47, 0.42, 0.40.\bar{k}_{\text{mc}}=59.6,\;108.2,\;206.2\hskip 10.00002pt\Rightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{\bar{k}_{\text{mc}}}{n}\approx 0.47,\;0.42,\;0.40.

Thus the certified fraction of retained keys decreases slowly with nn, yielding mean theoretical speedups of roughly 2.12.1–2.5×2.5\times while maintaining the target accuracy.

Discussion.

The experiment empirically validates the theoretical asymptotics: for a fixed tolerance ε\varepsilon, the expected certified fraction kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n remains nearly constant, confirming that the required sparsity grows linearly with sequence length. Although Δ\Delta-Search is too strict for flat early-layer distributions, MC-Search provides a tight, guaranteed bound and achieves predictable speedups. At longer contexts or higher ε\varepsilon, the ratio kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n is expected to decrease further, demonstrating substantial constant-factor reductions in effective quadratic attention cost in practice.

8.6 Accuracy–Efficiency Tradeoff (ε\varepsilon-Sweep)

Complementing the length scaling study, we now vary the TV tolerance ε\varepsilon to understand how certified sparsity responds to accuracy requirements.

Setup.

To quantify the empirical tradeoff between certified accuracy and sparsity, we fixed the requested Top-k=16k=16 and varied the error tolerance ε∈{10−3,×10−3, 10−2,×10−2,×10−2}\varepsilon\!\in\!\{10^{-3},\,5\!\times\!10^{-3},\,10^{-2},\,2\!\times\!10^{-2},\,5\!\times\!10^{-2}\} across sequence lengths n∈{128,256,512}n\!\in\!\{128,256,512\}. For each (n,ε)(n,\varepsilon), we measured the minimal mass-certified kmck_{\text{mc}} such that TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\!\leq\!\varepsilon, and the resulting mean speedup n/kmcn/k_{\text{mc}}.

Results.

Table 5 summarizes the mean certified truncation size and speedup. As ε\varepsilon relaxes, kmck_{\text{mc}} decreases roughly log-linearly, producing rapidly increasing speedups. At ε=0.01\varepsilon\!=\!0.01, the certified fraction kmc/nk_{\text{mc}}/n is nearly constant (≈0.4\approx 0.4) across all lengths, confirming the predicted linear scaling kε∝nk_{\varepsilon}\!\propto\!n and a substantially reduced effective quadratic attention cost. The deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate again proves too strict (0% pass rate), whereas the mass certificate achieves tight control of total variation.

Discussion.

The ε\varepsilon-sweep confirms the theoretical accuracy–efficiency curve: the certified fraction kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n decreases smoothly with tolerance, approximately following a Gaussian-tail law. For moderate tolerances (ε≈0.01\varepsilon\!\approx\!0.01–0.020.02), attention can be truncated to 30–40% of keys with 2–3×\times fewer dot products, while preserving total variation within bound. At relaxed tolerances (ε≥0.05\varepsilon\!\geq\!0.05), average speedups in these runs reach about 3–4×\times, revealing substantial headroom for certified Top-kk in long-context transformers. The empirical curves in Figure 2 illustrate this smooth tradeoff: the left panel shows mean speedup n/k¯mcn/\bar{k}_{\mathrm{mc}} versus ε\varepsilon, while the right panel reports the certified fraction k¯mc/n\bar{k}_{\mathrm{mc}}/n. Both are consistent with the Gaussian-tail law predicted in Section 6. Overall, the ε\varepsilon-sweep supports the asymptotic law kε/n≈Φc​(σ+Φ−1​(ε))k_{\varepsilon}/n\approx\Phi_{c}(\sigma+\Phi^{-1}(\varepsilon)) derived under the Gaussian model, indicating good alignment between theoretical and empirical trends.

8.7 Validation of Long-Context Scaling

To isolate very long-context behavior in a controlled setting, we now turn to synthetic Gaussian logits and examine how the certified sparsity ratio behaves as nn grows.

To verify that the certified sparsity ratio kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n remains stable as the context length increases, we simulated long attention logits ti∼𝒩⁡(0,1)t_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) for n∈{4096, 8192, 16384}n\in\{4096,\,8192,\,16384\} and a range of target tolerances ε\varepsilon. For each configuration we computed the minimal mass-certified kmck_{\text{mc}} per query such that the residual mass ∑i>kw(i)/∑iwi≤ε\sum_{i>k}w_{(i)}/\sum_{i}w_{i}\leq\varepsilon, where w(i)w_{(i)} denotes the ii-th largest exponential weight. The results, averaged over 200 Monte Carlo trials, are summarized below.

Across all tested lengths, the ratio kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n is effectively constant, validating the theoretical prediction that the required fraction of retained keys depends primarily on ε\varepsilon and not on nn. Moreover, the close agreement between empirical and theoretical values confirms that, for synthetic Gaussian logits, the asymptotic law of Section 6 provides an accurate quantitative description of the certified sparsity. Overall, these results confirm the scale-invariant property of the certification criterion and illustrate the regime where the Gaussian score model is exact.

8.8 Mid-Length Real-Text Evaluation and Head-Wise Heterogeneity

While Sections 8.5–8.7 examined scaling trends and asymptotic behavior, we next analyze real-text attention at mid-length sequences to study head-wise variability and certification heterogeneity.

Setup. We evaluated certified Top-kk truncation on real text using the bert-base-uncased model (output_attentions=True) over the WikiText-2 validation split. Sequences were tokenized into fixed windows of length n∈{128,256}n\in\{128,256\}, padded, and passed through the model in evaluation mode. For each query row we computed the exact attention probabilities, the diagnostic tail mass at fixed k=16k=16 (non-certified baseline), and the minimal mass-certified size kmck_{\mathrm{mc}} achieving TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon for ε∈{10−3,5×10−3,10−2,2×10−2,5×10−2}\varepsilon\in\{10^{-3},5\times 10^{-3},10^{-2},2\times 10^{-2},5\times 10^{-2}\}. We also applied the deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate from Section 7.1 by evaluating Δ=log⁡p(k)−log⁡p(k+1)\Delta=\log p_{(k)}-\log p_{(k+1)}, which equals the score gap s(k)−s(k+1)s_{(k)}-s_{(k+1)} under softmax normalization.

Aggregate behavior. Table 7 summarizes the mean certified sizes and speedups. The fixed-kk diagnostic shows that k=16k=16 is generally unsafe at these lengths: TVmean≈0.16\mathrm{TV}_{\mathrm{mean}}\approx 0.16 for n=128n=128 and ≈0.22\approx 0.22 for n=256n=256, well above typical ε\varepsilon values. In contrast, the mass certificate adapts kk to each distribution and guarantees TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon. At ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01, we obtain kmc,mean≈58.8k_{\mathrm{mc},\text{mean}}\approx 58.8 for n=128n=128 and ≈107.8\approx 107.8 for n=256n=256, corresponding to mean speedups n/kmc≈2.2×n/k_{\mathrm{mc}}\approx 2.2\times and 2.4×2.4\times, respectively. Relaxing ε\varepsilon yields monotonic reductions in kmck_{\mathrm{mc}} and rapid growth in speedup, consistent with the Gaussian-tail law derived in Section 6.

Head-wise heterogeneity. The head-wise analysis (Table 8) reveals substantial variation in sparsity across layers. Early heads exhibit diffuse attention (Δ¯≈0.04−0.07\overline{\Delta}\approx 0.04{-}0.07), yielding large kmck_{\mathrm{mc}} and modest speedups (≈1−2×\approx 1{-}2\times), whereas several mid-layer heads are strongly peaked and certify aggressively. For example, at n=128n=128 and ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01: Layer 2–Head 0 achieves certΔ≈76%\mathrm{cert}^{\Delta}\!\approx 76\%, Δ¯≈10.9\overline{\Delta}\!\approx 10.9, and kmc,mean≈1.1k_{\mathrm{mc,mean}}\!\approx 1.1 (∼120×\sim 120\times reduction); Layer 2–Head 9 attains similar values with ∼72×\sim 72\times reduction. At n=256n=256, Layer 2–Head 0 remains sharply peaked (certΔ≈64%\mathrm{cert}^{\Delta}\!\approx 64\%, kmc,mean≈1.1k_{\mathrm{mc,mean}}\!\approx 1.1, ∼238×\sim 238\times). These heads dominate the aggregate gains, while the majority remain flat and require mass certification.

Discussion. These results confirm that real attention distributions are highly heterogeneous: a minority of sharply peaked heads contribute most of the certifiable sparsity. The deterministic Δ\Delta-certificate succeeds primarily in such regimes, while the mass certificate provides universal guarantees elsewhere. A practical hybrid strategy is therefore: (i) attempt Δ\Delta-Search and accept if

Δ≥log⁡n−kk+log⁡1−εε;\Delta\;\geq\;\log\!\frac{n-k}{k}+\log\!\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon};

(ii) otherwise invoke MC-Search to minimally increase kk until TV≤ε\mathrm{TV}\leq\varepsilon. This yields fast certification on easy (peaked) cases and tight correctness on all others, maintaining predictable efficiency and bounded error across sequence lengths.

9 Conclusion and Outlook

We presented a unified mathematical framework and certified algorithms for Top-kk attention truncation. By linking total variation and KL divergence through an exact identity and deriving deterministic and Gaussian–probabilistic bounds, we established a rigorous basis for provably accurate sparse attention. The proposed Δk\Delta_{k}-Search and MC-Search algorithms translate these theoretical guarantees into practical selection rules that certify TV≤ε\operatorname{TV}\leq\varepsilon while achieving subquadratic complexity in sequence length.

Empirical evaluations on bert-base-uncased confirm the predictions of the theory: the certified fraction kε/nk_{\varepsilon}/n remains nearly constant across context sizes, and efficiency grows exponentially with tolerance ε\varepsilon. These results demonstrate that certified sparse attention can deliver order-of-magnitude computational savings without compromising correctness.

Future work will extend the framework to multi-head and multi-query regimes, investigate adaptive training with certified sparsity schedules, and integrate certified Top-kk modules into large-scale transformer inference engines. Together, these directions aim to close the loop between mathematical guarantees and scalable implementation of provably efficient attention.

Broader Impact and Limitations

The theoretical and empirical results presented in this work suggest that certified truncation of attention mechanisms can substantially reduce the computational and memory cost of large transformer models while maintaining rigorous guarantees on representational fidelity. Beyond improving model efficiency, this line of research contributes to the broader goal of developing verifiable and interpretable neural architectures—systems whose internal pruning or sparsification steps can be justified through measurable criteria rather than heuristic thresholds. Certified Top-kk truncation provides a formal link between model compression, probabilistic robustness, and differential privacy, indicating that sparsity can be reasoned about within a unified analytical framework rather than introduced as an ad hoc engineering choice.

Societal and practical impact.

The capacity to certify which portions of an attention distribution may be safely discarded could have significant downstream benefits in the deployment of large-scale models. Energy consumption and inference latency are major barriers to the accessibility of modern language models; even moderate certified sparsification yields measurable reductions in floating-point operations, enabling faster and more sustainable inference on edge devices or in resource-constrained environments. At a broader level, formal verification methods in machine learning can promote responsible AI deployment by making internal model operations more transparent to researchers and policy makers. Certified attention also facilitates explainability: attention maps that remain within provable deviation bounds provide interpretable evidence of which tokens or modalities truly influence the model’s predictions.

Limitations.

Several limitations temper the current results. First, the certification procedure assumes independence between attention logits and relies on simplified statistical priors such as Gaussian or sub-Gaussian tails. Real attention distributions observed in large pretrained models are heavier-tailed and context-dependent, leading to conservative or vacuous certificates in extreme regimes. Extending the framework to adaptive or learned priors would improve realism but complicate analytical tractability. Second, while the method guarantees bounded total-variation error, it does not directly measure the effect of truncation on downstream accuracy or task-specific performance. In practice, an acceptable ε\varepsilon depends on both theoretical tolerance and the semantic sensitivity of the task. Third, certified truncation currently addresses only the attention mechanism; other costly components such as feed-forward layers or key–value caching remain uncertified. Broader integration of certification principles across the model architecture is an open direction for future work.

Outlook.

Overall, certified Top-kk attention provides a foundation for provably efficient sequence models. Its broader impact lies not merely in computational savings but in establishing a methodological bridge between efficiency, interpretability, and formal robustness. Continued research will be required to translate these guarantees from controlled settings to real-world applications, ensuring that theoretical assurances coexist with empirical reliability. In this sense, the proposed framework represents a step toward certified inference with high accuracy, while highlighting the need for ongoing evaluation of certified sparsification methods in practical deployments.

A.1 Tail–Mass Identity (Lemma A.1)

Lemma A.1 (Tail–mass identity).

For Top-kk truncation as above,

TV⁡(P,P^)=∑i>kpi.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\sum_{i>k}p_{i}.
Proof.

Recall pi=esi∑j=1nesjp_{i}=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}} and p^i=esi∑j=1kesj\widehat{p}_{i}=\frac{e^{s_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{s_{j}}} for i≤ki\leq k (and 00 otherwise). By definition,

TV⁡(P,P^)=12​∑i=1n|pi−p^i|.\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|p_{i}-\widehat{p}_{i}|.

For i>ki>k, p^i=0\widehat{p}_{i}=0, hence |pi−p^i|=pi|p_{i}-\widehat{p}_{i}|=p_{i}. For i≤ki\leq k, the denominator of p^i\widehat{p}_{i} is smaller than that of pip_{i}, so p^i≥pi\widehat{p}_{i}\geq p_{i} and |pi−p^i|=p^i−pi|p_{i}-\widehat{p}_{i}|=\widehat{p}_{i}-p_{i}. Therefore

TV⁡(P,P^)=12​(∑i>kpi+∑i≤k(p^i−pi)).\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(\sum_{i>k}p_{i}+\sum_{i\leq k}(\widehat{p}_{i}-p_{i})\Big).

Because ∑i≤kp^i=1\sum_{i\leq k}\widehat{p}_{i}=1 and ∑i≤kpi=1−∑i>kpi\sum_{i\leq k}p_{i}=1-\sum_{i>k}p_{i},

∑i≤k(p^i−pi)=1−(1−∑i>kpi)=∑i>kpi.\sum_{i\leq k}(\widehat{p}_{i}-p_{i})=1-\Big(1-\sum_{i>k}p_{i}\Big)=\sum_{i>k}p_{i}.

Plugging in yields TV⁡(P,P^)=∑i>kpi\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=\sum_{i>k}p_{i}. ∎

A.2 Exact TV\operatorname{TV}–KL\operatorname{KL} Identity (Theorem A.2)

Theorem A.2 (Exact TV–KL identity).

For the distributions PP and P^\widehat{P} defined above,

KL(P^∥P)=log∑j=1nesj∑j=1kesj,TV(P,P^)=1−e−KL(P^∥P).\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)=\log\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}e^{s_{j}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{s_{j}}},\hskip 20.00003pt\operatorname{TV}(P,\widehat{P})=1-e^{-\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{P}\|P)}.
